planting.note: Set out divisions or container-grown plants in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones, into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Tokajer flowers heavily its first season and holds its color through Gulf Coast summer heat.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since rich or consistently damp ground promotes the crown rot that shortens the life of most blanket flowers. Tokajer stands out for its warm, marmalade-orange petals that darken toward a raspberry-red cone, a mango-and-burnt-sienna coloring that reads differently from the brighter red-and-yellow standard grandiflora forms. Its taller, somewhat sprawling stems benefit from being sited among neighboring perennials or ornamental grasses that can offer light support without shading it out. Deadhead spent blooms through the long summer season to keep new buds coming, and expect strong heat and drought tolerance once the plant is established.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Amber Wheels Blanket Flower (Frilled Gold and Red Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery transplants in spring into lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Amber Wheels was selected from a long-lived wild Colorado population and typically does not bloom heavily until its second season.

directions: Site in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since this selection was bred from a naturally long-lived wild population and rewards the same tough, infertile conditions its parent thrived in. Amber Wheels carries large, frilled deep-yellow ray petals held loosely around a contrasting amber-red center disc, giving the flower a spinning, pinwheel-like look distinct from flatter blanket flower cultivars. It grows notably taller and more robust than compact bedding gaillardias, so give it room among other sun perennials rather than crowding it to the front of a border. Established plants are markedly longer-lived than typical grandiflora hybrids, tolerate extended drought once rooted in, and shrug off deer and rabbit browsing.

common_name: Mesa Red Blanket Flower (Compact Solid-Red Gaillardia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mesa Red is an F1 hybrid that flowers uniformly from seed its first year without a cold treatment.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mesa Red is a companion to the AAS-winning Mesa Yellow, bred for the same compact, uniform, well-branched habit but carrying intense, solid red ray petals that hold their color without fading through the season. It blooms two to three weeks earlier than comparable seed-grown blanket flowers and continues from late spring into fall, with spent flowers giving way to attractive globe-shaped seed heads if left unshorn. The tight, upright mound resists wind and rain damage far better than older sprawling gaillardia types and needs no staking. As with other Mesa-series plants, sharp drainage is essential in humid Gulf Coast conditions to avoid crown rot.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox

common_name: Mesa Bicolor Blanket Flower (Compact Red-and-Yellow Gaillardia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mesa Bicolor is an F1 hybrid bred to flower uniformly from seed its first year without a cold treatment.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mesa Bicolor extends the compact, well-branched Mesa series into the traditional blanket-flower color pattern, with deep red-orange centers ringed by bright yellow-orange petal tips on a tidy, rounded mound under a foot tall. Its dense branching and short stature give it excellent resistance to wind and heavy rain compared to older, floppier gaillardia strains, and it needs no staking or shearing to stay tidy. Plants bloom continuously from late spring into fall, drawing bees and butterflies steadily through the hottest part of the season. Sharp drainage is essential, especially in humid Gulf Coast gardens, where wet feet lead quickly to crown rot.

common_name: SpinTop Red Blanket Flower (Dwarf Pinwheel Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones, into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; SpinTop Red stays under a foot tall and is well suited to containers as well as border edges.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, very well-drained soil; SpinTop Red is a dense, well-branched dwarf selection that sets many buds per stem, producing a fluffy profusion of solid orange-red flowers with prominent gold stamens and chocolate-brown cones. Its toothy, notched petal tips give each bloom a distinctive pinwheel texture that stands out from smoother-petaled blanket flower cultivars. The compact, low mound stays under 14 inches and works well massed along a sunny border edge or in mixed containers, where it flowers from spring through fall with only occasional deadheading. Once established it is very drought tolerant, but prompt drainage is essential through humid Gulf Coast summers to prevent crown rot.

common_name: SpinTop Orange Halo Blanket Flower (Dwarf Bicolor Pinwheel Gaillardia)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones, into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; SpinTop Orange Halo stays under a foot tall and suits containers as well as border edges.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, very well-drained soil; SpinTop Orange Halo carries toasty red-orange petals tipped with a glowing yellow band around a deep burgundy center dotted with yellow, giving each notch-tipped bloom a striking bicolor halo effect. Like its SpinTop series siblings, it is a dense, low, well-branched grower that sets multiple buds per stem for a long, heavy flowering display from spring through fall. The compact habit stays under 14 inches without staking, making it a strong choice for containers, rock gardens, or the front of a sunny border. Plants tolerate heat and drought well once established, but need sharp drainage to avoid crown rot in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
